questions.q: What does this lesson say about its own content before covering any specific regulation?
options: That it is a complete substitute for legal advice and covers every possible requirement
That the content is not legal advice, AI regulation moves quickly, and the goal is conceptual fluency rather than memorized clauses
That AI regulation never changes once written, so the details here will always be accurate
That compliance questions never require consulting an actual lawyer
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly hedges that it isn't legal advice and that specifics change, framing the goal as recognizing when real legal review is needed.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe GDPR's 'data minimization' principle, and what earlier lesson does it connect to?
options: Collecting and retaining only the personal data actually needed — the same principle behind Lesson 13's advice to omit what you don't need to keep in logs
A requirement to collect as much personal data as technically possible for future use
A rule that applies only to companies based in the United States
A principle that has nothing to do with any other lesson in this course
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties GDPR's data minimization to Lesson 13's logging guidance of omitting data that isn't needed.

questions.q: What is the core idea behind the EU AI Act's 'risk-tiering' approach, according to this lesson?
options: Every AI system faces identical obligations regardless of its use case
Only systems built after a certain date are regulated at all
Obligations scale with how much potential harm a system's specific use case carries, not with the underlying technology itself
Risk tiers are assigned randomly by a lottery system
questions.explain: The AI Act's risk-tiering scales obligations to the potential harm of the use case (e.g., hiring vs. a spam filter), not to the technology used.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the same underlying AI model could face very different compliance obligations?
options: Because compliance obligations are identical for every possible use case of a model
Because the model's obligations depend entirely on which programming language it was built with
Because risk-tiering means a model used for something like hiring (high risk) faces very different obligations than the same model used for something like game NPC dialogue (minimal risk)
Because only open-source models are ever subject to any regulation
questions.explain: Risk-tiering is based on use case, so the exact same model can land in a completely different obligation tier depending on how it's deployed.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect compliance back to the rest of the chapter's content (bias testing, PII handling, model cards)?
options: It argues compliance is a separate checkbox exercise entirely disconnected from engineering practices covered earlier
It claims none of the earlier lessons have any relevance to regulatory compliance
It frames compliance as largely asking for the same engineering discipline already built in this chapter, with legal consequences attached
It says compliance only applies to lessons about monitoring, not governance
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly says bias testing, PII handling, and model cards are close to what regulatory obligations ask for in practice, not a separate add-on.
